preparation.takeaway: A mixed panel finishes one page knowing the whole argument: insulation cannot protect kilovolt-class machines at altitude, dividing the bus inside the winding removes the physics, the same decision yields pole-count freedom and three per cent fault steps, the price is a 64 degree of freedom coupled co-design, and the grant buys that methodology plus 100 kW evidence.

The cascade: software pole count, about 3 per cent capability loss per fault, end-winding removal.
The price stated plainly: 32 coupled sections, 64 degrees of freedom, no existing methodology.
What the grant buys: methodology, controllability theory, scaled IC via a costed fabrication run, 100 kW validation.

parts.name: Crossing the line: the 50 V claim

preparation.takeaway: The reader watches the claim being derived rather than asserted: up to 1 kV composed magnetically along the open-end winding as 64 steps, 32 per end-face, so no insulation boundary ever sees more than about 16 V, a factor of twenty below the physical floor while a conventional kilovolt machine sits above cruise inception.

The bus is never delivered to the winding; it is composed by the winding.
The arithmetic shown: 1000 over 64 gives 15.6, written approximately 16 V.
Margin in both directions: twenty times below the 330 V floor; conventional 1 kV two to three times above cruise inception.
The autotransformer lineage above 99 per cent as the efficiency answer.
The dual identity: the IC is excitation source and switching element; the conductor is torque medium and distribution network.
The enabling die exists: 15.2 mm2 in 130 nm BCD, floating-domain gate control in the same process.

H4 thermal: monolithic ICs operate inside a 120 to 150 degrees Celsius winding within a junction class of 150 to 175 degrees Celsius.
RQ1 to RQ5 as filed, RQ4 expanded per the A3 answer.

Every electric drive ever deployed keeps the power converter and the machine winding as separate electrical objects, met at terminals, with insulation rated for the full bus. This programme will establish the foundations of the architecture that dissolves that partition: a pair of integrated circuits at every one of {{SLOTS}} stator slots, each driving its own winding section bilaterally across an open-end winding, with a bus of up to {{BUS_V}} DC composed magnetically along the machine as {{STEPS}} steps so that no section sees more than approximately {{SECT_V}} [PI TO CONFIRM: per-section envelope of 15 to 16 V derived from 1 kV across 64 steps]. Partial discharge at altitude is eliminated by architecture, pole count becomes a control variable so the gearbox leaves the drivetrain, and a single fault costs about three per cent of capability rather than a third. The price, and the science, is coupling: 32 sections sharing one core form a {{DOF}}-degree-of-freedom co-design problem with no existing methodology. The programme delivers that methodology, the controllability theory, a scaled per-slot IC through a costed fabrication run, and validation on a {{DEMO_KW}}, {{DEMO_RPM}} demonstrator. Word count: 196.

Electric aircraft promise quieter skies and an end to aviation's fossil-fuel dependence, and the United Kingdom has committed to net zero aviation by 2050. Standing in the way is a piece of engineering architecture so old that it is rarely questioned. In every electric vehicle, train and aircraft flying today, the electric motor and the power electronics that drive it are two separate objects. The electronics create high voltages; thick insulation protects the motor's copper windings from them; and the two meet at a set of terminals. That separation, invisible to passengers, sets the limits of what electric flight can be. It forces motors to carry insulation instead of useful copper. It leaves aircraft vulnerable to an effect called partial discharge, in which the thin air at cruising altitude allows tiny sparks to gnaw invisibly through insulation that passed every test on the ground. It means a single electrical fault can remove a third of a motor's output in an instant. And because a motor's natural speed is fixed by how it is wound, aircraft must often carry a gearbox, with its oil, its inspections and its own history of serious accidents. This programme will establish the foundations of a machine in which the separation no longer exists. Instead of one large converter feeding the whole motor, a pair of tiny silicon chips sits at every one of the motor's 32 slots, each driving its own small section of winding. The high supply voltage, up to a thousand volts, is never delivered to the winding at all; it is divided magnetically along the machine itself, so that no section of copper ever experiences more than about sixteen volts. Sixteen volts cannot spark at any altitude; the physics that erodes conventional insulation simply never begins. The consequences multiply. With every slot independently controlled, the motor's characteristics become software: it can reshape itself in flight to suit the propeller, so the gearbox disappears. If one section fails, the machine loses about three per cent of its capability rather than a third, and keeps flying predictably, which is exactly what new safety rules for electric vertical take-off aircraft demand. Reliability, efficiency and simplicity improve together, because they all flow from the same design decision rather than being traded against one another. The research challenge, and the reason this needs a university programme, is that the thirty-two sections share one magnetic core and therefore influence each other. Designing and controlling sixty-four interacting quantities at once, across electromagnetics, electronics, heat and control, is a scientific problem no one has yet had to solve, because the old separation kept those disciplines conveniently apart. The team spans exactly those disciplines: the microchips already exist in prototype form and have been published, an earlier converter from the same family has already driven an industrial motor in the laboratory, and the programme will build and test a full 100-kilowatt demonstrator, the size of motor now flying on electric air-taxi prototypes. The work is supported by Eaton and Airbus, and its results, the design methods, the control theory and the measured evidence, will be published openly. If it succeeds, it gives the UK the foundations of a propulsion technology that is safer at altitude, simpler to certify, lighter to fly and cheaper to maintain than anything the old architecture allows.

That separation, invisible to passengers, sets the limits of what electric flight can be. It forces motors to carry insulation instead of useful copper. It leaves aircraft vulnerable to an effect called partial discharge, in which the thin air at cruising altitude allows tiny sparks to gnaw invisibly through insulation that passed every test on the ground. It means a single electrical fault can remove a third of a motor's output in an instant. And because a motor's natural speed is fixed by how it is wound, aircraft must often carry a gearbox, with its oil, its inspections and its own history of serious accidents. This programme will establish the foundations of a machine in which the separation no longer exists. Instead of one large converter feeding the whole motor, a pair of tiny silicon chips sits at every one of the motor's 32 slots, each driving its own small section of winding. The high supply voltage, up to a thousand volts, is never delivered to the winding at all; it is divided magnetically along the machine itself, so that no section of copper ever experiences more than about sixteen volts. Sixteen volts cannot spark at any altitude; the physics that erodes conventional insulation simply never begins. The consequences multiply. With every slot independently controlled, the motor's characteristics become software: it can reshape itself in flight to suit the propeller, so the gearbox disappears. If one section fails, the machine loses about three per cent of its capability rather than a third, and keeps flying predictably, which is exactly what new safety rules for electric vertical take-off aircraft demand. Reliability, efficiency and simplicity improve together, because they all flow from the same design decision rather than being traded against one another. The research challenge, and the reason this needs a university programme, is that the thirty-two sections share one magnetic core and therefore influence each other. Designing and controlling sixty-four interacting quantities at once, across electromagnetics, electronics, heat and control, is a scientific problem no one has yet had to solve, because the old separation kept those disciplines conveniently apart. The team spans exactly those disciplines: the microchips already exist in prototype form and have been published, an earlier converter from the same family has already driven an industrial motor in the laboratory, and the programme will build and test a full 100-kilowatt demonstrator, the size of motor now flying on electric air-taxi prototypes. The work is supported by Eaton and Airbus, and its results, the design methods, the control theory and the measured evidence, will be published openly. If it succeeds, it gives the UK the foundations of a propulsion technology that is safer at altitude, simpler to certify, lighter to fly and cheaper to maintain than anything the old architecture allows. variants.text: The partition's costs arrive as four constraint families. First, insulation and partial discharge (PD). In kilovolt-class form-wound machines only some 40 to 60 per cent of the slot is conductor; the rest is insulation and unavoidable gap [9]. At cruise altitude the problem sharpens from expensive to dangerous: partial discharge inception voltage (PDIV) roughly halves from sea level, to approximately {{PDIV_CRUISE}} near {{ALT_KPA}}, approaching the pressure-independent floor of about {{PD_FLOOR}} set by the Paschen minimum for air [5], [6]. A machine that passes every ground qualification can discharge continuously at altitude, eroding its insulation from the first flight, and fast wide-bandgap switching sharpens the turn-to-turn stress it must survive [7]. Second, the gearbox. Pole count is wired into the winding, so the machine has one torque-speed characteristic while the propulsor needs another, and the translation is mechanical: an oil system, a thirty-minute loss-of-lubrication endurance requirement and mandatory chip detection under CS-29 [29], a documented fatigue accident record [30], [31], and half to one per cent of transmitted power lost per mesh. The certified electric aircraft sector is already fleeing the component where it can: Joby abandoned gearing, Beta drives direct, and Archer's geared Midnight stands as the honest live counterexample. Third, fault fragility, and the honest price of the remedy. Three phases from one inverter lose roughly a third of output in a step when one phase opens. The field's answer is the multiphase machine [10], [11]: five phases retain about 70 per cent with one phase open, dual three-phase about 50 per cent. But the softening is bought by duplicating inverter channels, gate drives, isolated supplies, sensing and protection, diluting the power density it defends, and the winding still sits at bus voltage with its pole count fixed. Fourth, end-windings: copper outside the core, the machine's hot spot and least productive conductor [8], carrying an aspect-ratio-dependent share of winding resistance that reaches 50 per cent and more in short stacks. Four literatures, four mitigation communities, one unquestioned assumption underneath. Word count: 336.

This programme will establish the architecture in which the bus never reaches the insulation at all. One pair of integrated circuits (ICs) sits at every one of {{SLOTS}} stator slots, each pair driving its own winding section bilaterally across an open-end winding. The bus, up to {{BUS_V}} DC, is not delivered to the winding and insulated against; it is composed magnetically along the machine, on the autotransformer principle the group has operated above 99 per cent efficiency [4], as {{STEPS}} voltage steps, {{STEPS_SIDE}} at each end-face, so that no winding section ever sees more than approximately {{SECT_V}} [PI TO CONFIRM: per-section envelope of 15 to 16 V derived from 1 kV across 64 steps]. The comparison is stark in both directions. A conventional machine on a {{BUS_V}} bus sits a factor of two to three above measured cruise-altitude inception [5]; every section of this machine sits roughly twenty times below the physical floor of about {{PD_FLOOR}} that no pressure can lower [6]. The IC is simultaneously the machine's per-slot excitation source and the converter's switching element; the winding conductor is simultaneously the torque-producing medium and the converter's voltage-distribution network. The enabling die exists: the group's per-slot drive infrastructure occupies {{DIE_MM2}} in a {{NODE}} process [1], with floating-domain gate control in the same process [2]. The converter as a separate object dissolves into the machine. Word count: 240.

One decision, independently programmable current in every slot, and each benefit follows without being added. Partial discharge is eliminated by architecture rather than insulation, because the voltage that would cause discharge never arrives at any insulation boundary. Pole count becomes a software parameter: {{SLOTS}} independently driven sections synthesise any spatial harmonic set up to 16 pole pairs, so the torque-speed characteristic is retuned to the propulsor at every operating point and the gearbox, its oil, its inspection schedule and its failure mode leave the drivetrain; prior variable-pole work proved the principle at terminal level over a shared bus [20], [21], and this architecture generalises it to full spatial resolution. Fault tolerance arrives without duplication: the effective phase count equals the section count, so nothing is added to obtain redundancy, and the loss of one section removes, to first order, about three per cent of the ampere-conductor capability, degrading continuously in exactly the partial, bounded and predictable manner the certification framework for vertical-lift aircraft expects [23], where five-phase machines retain about 70 per cent and dual three-phase about 50 per cent at far greater channel cost [10], [11]. End-windings are structurally eliminated, since conductors terminate at IC modules at the end-faces where cooling is most effective [8]. Adiabatic zero-voltage switching gives inherently smooth per-section transitions, and the external converter, its cabinet, busbars and cables disappear from the mass budget. The price is the programme's central scientific problem. The {{SLOTS}} sections share one magnetic core, so they are {{SLOTS}} coupled actuators, and the design space becomes a {{DOF}}-degree-of-freedom co-design spanning winding electromagnetics, circuit envelope, thermal path and control, a problem with no existing methodology because the partition allowed those disciplines to remain separate. That co-design framework, not the demonstrator machine, is the contribution. Its open questions are the research: whether adiabatic soft switching survives an inductive back-EMF source, whether {{DOF}}-degree-of-freedom control remains stable and controllable under inter-slot coupling or whether coupling imposes a fundamental limit, and how IC modules survive thermally inside a winding at {{WIND_C}} against a junction limit near {{JUNC_C}}. Word count: 344.

Honesty about the closest prior art defines what is claimed. Slot-level converter granularity exists: the intelligent stator cage drive demonstrated one half-bridge per slot bar with electronic pole changing in a 110 kW vehicle drive [13]. Sub-bus module voltages exist: the Wisconsin integrated modular motor drive series-stacks gallium nitride converter modules so each sees a fraction of the DC link [14]. Bilateral feed exists in open-end winding drives [12], and electronic pole changing at terminal level exists [13], [20], [21]. None of these derives safe voltages from a high-voltage bus inside the machine. The stator cage drive is supplied externally at 48 V and pays for it in kiloampere system currents; the Wisconsin stack divides the bus capacitively, outside the winding, per pole, unilaterally, hard-switched. What has never existed, and what this programme will establish, is the conjunction: bilateral open-end drive at every slot, magnetic composition of a bus of up to {{BUS_V}} into sections of approximately {{SECT_V}} by the winding itself, monolithic IC integration of the complete per-slot drive, elimination of partial discharge at altitude by design rather than by insulation, and adiabatic soft switching throughout. The scientific contribution is the co-design and control theory of 32 magnetically coupled actuators sharing one core, a {{DOF}}-degree-of-freedom problem for which no methodology exists, delivered with a property-by-property differentiation against every neighbouring architecture. Word count: 219.

Three independent developments make this the moment, and none of them existed together before the current cycle. The silicon is complete: the group's per-slot drive infrastructure on a single die is published [1], floating-domain gate control in the same process is in press [2], and the doctoral work that closed the platform's converter lineage demonstrated a binary-tree converter driving a 400 V industrial induction machine under closed-loop control while naming inductive and motor loads at scale as the explicit next step [3]; this programme is that step, taken at per-slot resolution. The certification framework now rewards the architecture's failure behaviour: the special condition governing vertical take-off and landing aircraft requires continued safe flight and landing after failure of a lift or thrust unit [23], which is precisely what a drive that loses three per cent per fault, rather than a third, is built to satisfy. And the electrical environment is moving toward this proposal, not away from it: 270 V DC is standardised military practice and flies today on production aircraft [28], and distribution voltages continue to rise with propulsion power toward the kilovolt class this architecture is designed to tame. Foundational work at technology readiness levels 1 to 3 must begin now if UK capability is to meet that convergence rather than follow it. Word count: 219.

The United Kingdom has committed, through the Jet Zero Strategy, to net zero aviation by 2050 [24], and the propulsion architectures that reach certification in the 2030s are being decided in research programmes now. The economic stakes are quantified from two directions. PwC's assessment of advanced air mobility estimates up to 2.1 billion pounds of annual UK socioeconomic benefit by 2040 from that sector alone [26], while the Department for Transport's Future of Flight Action Plan projects a 45 billion pound boost to the UK economy by 2030 from the wider drone and electric aviation economy [25]; the two figures measure different scopes and both depend on airworthy electric propulsion. The sector employs approximately {{JOBS_UK}} people in UK aerospace [27]. This programme concentrates value where the UK is genuinely strong: mixed-signal power IC design, electrical machine research and certification expertise, and it trains researchers, including a doctoral student co-supervised with industry [PI TO CONFIRM: co-funded studentship agreement], in exactly the cross-disciplinary co-design capability the partition has so far made unnecessary and the future makes essential. Word count: 175.

This is a technology readiness level (TRL) 1 to 3 programme. Its deliverables are the coupled electromagnetic, circuit, thermal and control co-design methodology, the controllability theory of magnetically coupled per-slot actuation, the scaled per-slot IC, and validated evidence from a {{DEMO_KW}}, {{DEMO_RPM}} demonstrator operating from a bus of up to {{BUS_V}}. It is pre-competitive by construction: the theory is platform-agnostic and publishable, and no single company can appropriate a design methodology that redefines the boundary between two industries' products, which is precisely why industry supports this work but will not fund its foundations. Adjacent, separately funded industrial programmes in the group's orbit evidence the translation environment awaiting these outputs while implying no commitment to this proposal. EPSRC support is the mechanism by which the foundational layer becomes UK public capability rather than a single supplier's advantage. Word count: 140.

Four hypotheses structure the programme. H1: a machine winding can serve as the magnetic voltage-distribution network of its own drive, composing a bus of up to {{BUS_V}} DC into {{STEPS}} steps so that no section exceeds approximately {{SECT_V}}, while simultaneously producing torque. H2: adiabatic zero-voltage switching (ZVS), demonstrated by the group against capacitive loads, survives an inductive back-electromotive-force source. H3: the {{DOF}}-degree-of-freedom (DOF) control problem posed by {{SLOTS}} magnetically coupled sections is stable and controllable at full slot count, or the conditions under which coupling imposes a fundamental limit can be stated and proven. H4: monolithic drive integrated circuits (ICs) can operate inside a winding environment of {{WIND_C}} within a junction limit near {{JUNC_C}}. Five research questions carry these hypotheses. RQ1: what winding geometry admits bilateral end-face IC access, kilovolt magnetic composition and multi-harmonic excitation, and whether 32 or 36 slots is the correct resolution. RQ2: under what conditions adiabatic ZVS holds against an inductive source. RQ3: what transient per-slot voltages arise during switching, faults and pole transitions, and whether they remain below inception thresholds with margin. RQ4: how {{DOF}}-DOF loss-minimising control is formulated, how fast post-fault re-optimisation can act, and under what conditions the coupled system is controllable at full slot count, including whether coupling imposes a fundamental limit. RQ5: what coupled thermal behaviour and packaging permits H4. Objectives: O1, deliver the co-design methodology and the RQ1 winding; O2, deliver the scaled per-slot IC through a costed fabrication run; O3, deliver the RQ4 control framework with proofs and hardware validation; O4, demonstrate {{DEMO_KW}} at {{DEMO_RPM}} from a bus of up to {{BUS_V}} with discharge-free operation verified at altitude-representative pressure; O5, demonstrate electronic pole reconfiguration and single-section fault ride-through above {{RIDE_PCT}} of capability. Word count: 296.

T1.1 (M1 to M6) fixes the machine topology: a rotor without a committed pole count, with cage and synchronous reluctance candidates traded against the pole programme, and the slot-count decision between 32 slots, which keeps the {{STEPS}}-step voltage ladder binary-tree native, and 36 slots, which offers a richer pole-divisor set at the cost of a hybrid ladder stage. The methodology is co-design under coupling, built and validated in three strands. The modelling strand constructs a unified state-space in which the {{SLOTS}} winding sections appear simultaneously as electromagnetic actuators, converter voltage steps, thermal sources and control channels, with inter-slot magnetic coupling retained rather than diagonalised away; model order and structure are themselves research outputs, since no existing formulation spans the four domains. The hardware strand advances on two benches: the group's existing rotating bench, on which a binary-tree converter of the same family already drives a 400 V industrial induction machine closed-loop [3], hosts early coupled-control and soft-switching experiments from month 6, de-risking the second bench, the {{SLOTS}}-slot, {{DEMO_KW}} demonstrator, which validates the framework at full scale. The measurement strand closes the loop: partial-discharge testing of winding coupons at altitude-representative pressure near {{ALT_KPA}}, calorimetric and electrical efficiency measurement, thermal imaging of in-slot modules, and fault-injection campaigns feed measured parameters back into the models so that the delivered methodology is measurement-informed rather than idealised. The programme stands on a completed silicon and converter lineage. The group's published per-slot drive integrated circuit integrates the complete drive infrastructure on a {{DIE_MM2}} die in {{NODE}}, operating at 2 A and approximately 26 V from DC to 5 kHz, with measured die temperatures of 50 to 66 degrees Celsius under loaded 5 kHz operation and a modelled total loss of 1.522 W at 2 A and 10 kHz [1]; it is a hard-switched device, and its role here is the integration precedent, not the switching regime. The adiabatic regime has its own lineage: the group's DC autotransformer demonstrated magnetic voltage distribution above 99 per cent efficiency [4], and the doctoral work that closed the converter family showed an eight-tap core composing 400 V from 50 V modules at 98.8 per cent in autotransformer mode, holding an unloaded tap firmly at its nominal level under stepped loading, and, decisively, drove a 4 kW-rated 400 V industrial induction machine on a back-to-back bench under closed-loop control [3]. That thesis lineage names experimental evaluation with inductive and motor loads at scale as its explicit future work, and states that a discrete realisation of per-slot infrastructure would exceed the machine's own volume. Integrated motor drives shorten the converter-machine partition by relocating an intact inverter onto the housing [15], [16], [17]; this programme dissolves the partition, which is the difference between packaging and architecture. This programme raises no human-participant, animal or personal-data issues; its responsible-innovation questions are real nonetheless, and the team addresses them through the AREA framework of anticipate, reflect, engage and act. The central issue is dual use. High-power-density, gearless, fault-tolerant electric propulsion is pursued for civil decarbonisation, and the same properties are of evident interest to defence and to uncrewed platforms whose uses the team cannot control. The team's position is engagement rather than denial: the underlying physics and the co-design methodology will publish regardless of this programme, so the responsible course is to develop them in the open, within UK governance, with deliberate screening. Concretely, the team will operate a pre-publication dual-use review for every output, drawing on UCL's research governance and export-control compliance processes to assess whether any specific result requires restriction under UK strategic export control legislation before release; will keep the published methodology at the level of design science rather than platform-specific engineering; and will engage the industrial partners, both experienced in aerospace governance, in that screening [PI TO CONFIRM: any partner-specific review arrangements]. The anticipated outcome, based on the technology readiness level 1 to 3 character of the outputs, is open release, and the mechanism exists for the exceptions. Environmental responsibility is intrinsic to the programme's purpose, an enabling technology for the Jet Zero commitment, and is also applied to its conduct: the machine topology deliberately keeps a rotor without permanent magnets among the leading candidates, holding open a rare-earth-free outcome, the demonstrator and its silicon are designed for reuse across the group's onward research rather than as disposable artefacts, and laboratory energy use in the {{DEMO_KW}} campaigns is recovered where the back-to-back configuration permits. Research integrity follows UCL policy: preregistered measurement protocols for the validation matrix, open datasets at the final milestones, and honest reporting of the negative branch of every research question, including any proven fundamental limit under RQ4, which the team regards as a publishable success rather than a failure. The team's development responsibilities are treated as part of responsible innovation: the postdoctoral researchers and the co-funded doctoral student are trained across all four coupled disciplines, recruitment follows UCL's equality, diversity and inclusion practice, and the programme's public summary and outreach present the work's limits as plainly as its promise. Every electric machine ever flown obeys a partition so old it has become invisible: the power converter makes the voltages, the winding makes the torque, and an insulation system stands between the two, rated for the full bus. As propulsion power rises, that bus is climbing toward the kilovolt class, and every consequence of the partition climbs with it. The insulation thickens and takes slot area from copper. The winding must be qualified against partial discharge in air whose breakdown strength collapses at altitude. The converter remains a separate mass of silicon, busbars and cable. The pole count stays frozen in the winding pattern, so a gearbox translates between what the machine does and what the propulsor needs. Reviewers of this proposal will recognise each of these costs individually, because each has its own literature, its own mitigation community and its own incremental progress. This programme will establish what happens when the assumption beneath all four is removed at once: when one pair of integrated circuits (ICs) sits at every stator slot and the converter, as a separate object, ceases to exist. An aircraft propulsion motor that cannot suffer partial discharge at any altitude, that loses about three per cent of its capability to any single fault instead of a third, and that needs no gearbox because its pole count is a control variable, is not available at any price today. The obstacle is not materials or devices; it is a partition. Since the first drive was built, the power converter and the machine winding have been separate electrical objects, met at terminals, with insulation rated for the full bus standing between them. This programme will establish the foundations of the architecture that removes their common cause: a pair of integrated circuits (ICs) at every stator slot, and no converter anywhere else. data.text:
An aircraft propulsion motor that cannot suffer partial discharge at any altitude, that loses about three per cent of its capability to any single fault instead of a third, and that needs no gearbox because its pole count is a control variable, is not available at any price today. The obstacle is not materials or devices; it is a partition. Since the first drive was built, the power converter and the machine winding have been separate electrical objects, met at terminals, with insulation rated for the full bus standing between them. Every expert reading this knows the four costs of that arrangement: insulation displacing copper from the slot, discharge inception falling toward the bus voltage at cruise altitude, a step loss of output when a phase fails, and a mechanical gearbox translating a frozen pole count into the speed the propulsor needs. Each cost has its own literature and its own mitigation community. This programme will establish the foundations of the architecture that removes their common cause: a pair of integrated circuits (ICs) at every stator slot, and no converter anywhere else. Word count: 178.

Every electric machine ever flown obeys a partition so old it has become invisible: the power converter makes the voltages, the winding makes the torque, and an insulation system stands between the two, rated for the full bus. As propulsion power rises, that bus is climbing toward the kilovolt class, and every consequence of the partition climbs with it. The insulation thickens and takes slot area from copper. The winding must be qualified against partial discharge in air whose breakdown strength collapses at altitude. The converter remains a separate mass of silicon, busbars and cable. The pole count stays frozen in the winding pattern, so a gearbox translates between what the machine does and what the propulsor needs. Reviewers of this proposal will recognise each of these costs individually, because each has its own literature, its own mitigation community and its own incremental progress. This programme will establish what happens when the assumption beneath all four is removed at once: when one pair of integrated circuits (ICs) sits at every stator slot and the converter, as a separate object, ceases to exist.
